The fleeing prophet meets sailors who try to save him

The foreign sailors behave better than the prophet. They pray while he sleeps (verses 5–6). He tells them to throw him overboard. Verse 13 says they rowed hard for land instead. They risked themselves for the man who had endangered them. In verse 14 they ask not to be guilty of his blood. Verse 16 ends with the sailors worshiping the LORD.
A rescued voice thanks the God it tried to flee

Jonah’s prayer is a psalm of thanks. He speaks it inside the fish, which he counts as his rescue. He says nothing about Nineveh or about running away. In verse 8 he looks down on those who worship idols. The sailors of chapter 1 have just worshiped more truly than he did. Verse 9 ends, “Salvation belongs to the LORD.” In chapter 4 he resents that truth when Nineveh receives it.
A brief warning produces a citywide change

Jonah’s message in verse 4 is one sentence with no offer of mercy. The whole city responds, from the king down. Verse 8 defines what turning means. Each person must leave his evil way and the violence in his hands. The king presumes nothing and says God may relent (verse 9). Verse 10 says God saw their works. Jeremiah 18:7–8 states the rule that a warned nation may be spared.
Concern for a plant meets concern for a whole city

Verse 2 finally explains why Jonah ran. He knew God’s mercy and did not want Nineveh to receive it. He quotes Exodus 34:6 as a complaint. The plant shows what Jonah cares about. He pities a vine that gave him shade for a day. God’s question in verse 11 sets that beside a whole city. The book ends with the question, and Jonah gives no answer.
